title: Best Class 12 Maths Books (Boards + JEE): Which to Buy and How to Combine Them + Free Quiz
meta_title: Best Class 12 Maths Books (Boards + JEE) + Free Quiz
meta_desc: Which Class 12 maths books to actually buy for boards vs JEE, NCERT plus Exemplar, RD Sharma, Cengage and Arihant, how to combine them, plus a free quiz.
excerpt: A shelf of six maths books does not raise your score — the right two, used in the right order, does. Here is exactly which Class 12 maths books to buy for boards and for JEE, and how to combine them without drowning.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Last April a Class 12 student from Jaipur brought me a photo of her study desk. Stacked on it were six Class 12 maths books — NCERT, RD Sharma, two different Arihant titles, a Cengage volume, and a ‘15 sample papers’ book — and her question was heartbreakingly common: ‘Sir, which one do I actually read?’ She owned more pages than she could finish in three years, let alone three months. The uncomfortable truth about Class 12 maths books is that owning more of them lowers your score, not raises it. The winners finish two books properly; the strugglers own eight and finish none.

So this guide is not a wish-list. It is about choosing the two or three Class 12 maths books that match your goal — boards, JEE, or both — and combining them in an order that does not leave you scattered.

Start here: NCERT is non-negotiable

Whatever your target, the NCERT Class 12 Mathematics textbook is book number one and it is not optional. The CBSE board paper is built almost entirely on NCERT examples and exercises, and a large slice of JEE Main is direct application of the same concepts. Before you spend a rupee on anything else, every solved example and every exercise question — including the Miscellaneous Exercise — should be under your belt. You can download it free from the official NCERT site or buy the printed set for a couple of hundred rupees.

The one add-on almost everyone should get

Pair NCERT with the NCERT Exemplar. This is the single most underused book on most desks. Its problems are a genuine notch harder than the textbook, they are the bridge between board-level and JEE-level thinking, and CBSE itself sometimes lifts higher-order questions from a similar mould. For a boards-only student, NCERT plus Exemplar is honestly close to sufficient.

If your goal is boards only

Do not over-buy. For a student aiming at a strong board percentage without JEE, three resources cover everything:

  • NCERT textbook — the spine. Master it end to end.
  • A step-by-step NCERT solution book — so you can check your working the moment you get stuck, instead of guessing at a method the book already teaches.
  • RD Sharma (Class 12) — only if you finish NCERT early and want more drill. Its strength is sheer volume of graded practice; its weakness is that it is enormous and easy to get lost in. Use it selectively, chapter by weak chapter, not cover to cover.

That is it. A boards student who finishes NCERT and Exemplar, checks work against solutions, and dips into RD Sharma for weak topics will out-score the student juggling five reference books every time.

If your goal is JEE (or boards + JEE)

Here the reference books earn their place — but only after NCERT, never instead of it. The most trusted names among serious JEE aspirants are consistent year after year:

  • Cengage Mathematics (G. Tewani series) — excellent theory build-up plus objective practice, ideal if you learn best from a book that explains before it drills.
  • Arihant ‘Skills in Mathematics’ (Amit M. Agarwal) — strong topic-wise depth, good for pushing a single chapter to JEE Advanced level.
  • Objective-type / previous-year JEE compilations — for pattern recognition and speed under a timer, once concepts are solid.

Pick one main reference series and stick with it. Cengage and Arihant both cover the syllabus fully; owning both and reading neither is the classic trap. Add a previous-year question bank on top, and you have a complete JEE maths stack.

The Class 12 maths books, side by side

BookBest forUse it when
NCERT textbookEveryone (boards + JEE base)First, always — before any reference
NCERT ExemplarHigher-order boards + JEE bridgeAfter the textbook exercises
NCERT solution bookChecking working, self-studyAlongside daily NCERT practice
RD SharmaExtra board-level drillOnly for weak chapters, if time allows
Cengage / ArihantJEE depth and objectivesAfter NCERT is solid, pick one series

How to combine them without drowning

Order beats quantity. The sequence that works for almost every student is the same: NCERT textbook → NCERT Exemplar → reference book → previous-year papers. Finish each layer before you open the next. A student who half-reads four books at once knows a little about everything and can solve nothing under exam pressure; a student who completes NCERT, then Exemplar, then one reference, builds real depth.

Here is the counter-intuitive bit I keep repeating to parents: the second pass through NCERT teaches you more than the first pass through a shiny new reference book. Repetition on a book you already half-know compounds; a fresh book resets you to zero. If you are choosing between buying a fifth book and re-doing the dotted questions in NCERT, re-do NCERT.

Avoiding book-overload — a quick gut-check

Before buying any Class 12 maths book, ask three questions. Have I finished NCERT and Exemplar? Do I have a specific gap this book fills that my current books do not? Will I realistically finish at least half of it before the exam? If the answer to any of these is no, keep your money. A thin book you finish always beats a thick book you abandon.

Try the quiz, then get the solutions

Below is a short, free quiz drawn straight from Class 12 topics — calculus, algebra, vectors and probability — so you can see which chapters still need work before you decide what to buy. Try it, then read the explanations for anything you miss. And when you want fully worked, step-by-step solutions to sit beside your NCERT while you practise, the Class 12 Mathematics NCERT Solution Book in the box below gives you exactly that.

quiz.title: Class 12 Maths Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight questions across calculus, algebra, vectors and probability at Class 12 level. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.

questions.q: Which book should a Class 12 student master before buying any reference book?
questions.explanation: NCERT is the base for both boards and JEE Main. Reference books add value only after the NCERT textbook and its exercises are solid.

questions.q: What is the derivative of cos(x) with respect to x?
questions.explanation: The derivative of cos(x) is −sin(x), a standard result from Continuity and Differentiability.
The antiderivative of 2x is x², plus the constant of integration C, since d/dx(x²) = 2x.

questions.q: If A is a 3×3 matrix with det(A) = 4, then det(3A) equals:
questions.explanation: For an n×n matrix, det(kA) = kⁿ det(A). Here 3³ × 4 = 27 × 4 = 108.

questions.q: A fair die is rolled once. What is the probability of getting a number greater than 4?
questions.explanation: The outcomes greater than 4 are 5 and 6 — two of six faces, so 2/6 = 1/3.

questions.q: The dot product of the vectors 2i + j + 2k and i + 3j + k is:
The principal value of cos⁻¹(0) is:
questions.explanation: cos(π/2) = 0, and π/2 lies in the principal range [0, π], so cos⁻¹(0) = π/2.

questions.q: The degree of the differential equation d²y/dx² + 3(dy/dx)² + y = 0 is:
questions.explanation: Degree is the power of the highest-order derivative when the equation is polynomial in derivatives. The highest derivative here, d²y/dx², appears to the first power, so the degree is 1.

faq.q: Which is the best maths book for Class 12 boards?
faq.a: The NCERT textbook, without question — the CBSE paper is built almost entirely on its examples and exercises. Add the NCERT Exemplar for higher-order questions, and a step-by-step solution book to check your working. That trio covers the board syllabus; RD Sharma is optional extra drill for weak chapters only.

faq.q: Is NCERT enough for Class 12 maths, or do I need reference books?
faq.a: For boards, NCERT plus Exemplar is close to sufficient. For JEE you need one reference series on top — but only after NCERT is solid, never instead of it. The mistake is buying references first and treating NCERT as revision; it should be the foundation you build on.

faq.q: Which book is best for Class 12 maths for JEE?
faq.a: After NCERT and Exemplar, most serious aspirants use either the Cengage series (G. Tewani) or Arihant’s Skills in Mathematics (Amit M. Agarwal). Pick one and finish it — both cover the full syllabus. Add a previous-year JEE question bank for speed and pattern practice.

faq.q: In what order should I combine my Class 12 maths books?
faq.a: NCERT textbook first, then NCERT Exemplar, then one reference book, then previous-year papers. Finish each layer before opening the next. Reading four books at once leaves you shallow everywhere; completing them in sequence builds real depth.
